notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum insertions needed to clear a Zuma board by removing runs of at least three matching balls.
Idea: Try every hand-ball insertion position, shrink all newly formed removable runs, and memoize board/hand states.
Technique and why it applies: shrink repeatedly scans for a run of length at least three and removes it until no more runs disappear. The recursive helper explores each remaining hand ball at every position and chooses the minimum move count.
Invariant: lookup stores the best known result for each tuple(board), tuple(hand) state.
Edge cases: Empty board returns zero; a nonempty board with no hand balls returns infinity and is converted to -1. Repeated collections imports are redundant but harmless.
Complexity: The state space and branching are combinatorial; worst-case time and memo space are exponential in board and hand sizes. shrink itself may rescan the board repeatedly.

Task and constraints: Return all distinct nondecreasing subsequences of nums that contain at least two elements.
Idea: Backtrack through later indices, adding a value only when it is at least the last selected value and has not been used at the current recursion depth.
Technique and why it applies: Each recursive call emits a copy of seq when its length reaches two. The local lookup set avoids generating duplicate branches for equal values at the same position depth.
Invariant: seq is a nondecreasing subsequence of the prefix positions selected so far, and pos restricts future choices to later indices.
Edge cases: Duplicate values may appear in a valid sequence, but identical next values are explored only once per recursion level. The input is not modified.
Complexity: There can be O(2^n) subsequences and copying each may cost O(n), so O(n·2^n) time is a reasonable bound. Recursion uses O(n) stack space plus output storage.

Task and constraints: Find the rectangle dimensions for a given area, with length at least width and their difference minimized.
Idea: Start near the square root of area and search downward for the largest divisor.
Technique and why it applies: The closest factor pair has its smaller factor as large as possible without exceeding sqrt(area). Once a divisor i is found, area/i is the matching length.
Invariant: Each tested i is a candidate width, and no larger candidate below or equal to the square root has been skipped.
Edge cases: area=0 returns [0,0] because mySqrt returns zero and the loop is skipped, though the standard problem requires positive area. The custom square-root method uses a tolerance of 0.9 and may stop with a rough estimate.
Complexity: The divisor search is O(sqrt(area)) in the worst case; the Newton-style estimate uses iterative floating-point arithmetic. Auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return [length,width] for a rectangle of the given area with the smallest possible difference and length >= width.
Idea: Begin at floor(sqrt(area)) and decrease width until it divides area evenly.
Technique and why it applies: The factor closest to the square root gives the most square-like rectangle. The first divisor found while decreasing from sqrt(area) therefore minimizes the dimension difference.
Invariant: All widths larger than the current w have already been ruled out as non-divisors.
Edge cases: area must be positive; for zero, w becomes zero and the modulo operation would fail. For positive area, math.sqrt supplies a starting estimate.
Complexity: Computing the square root is O(1) under fixed-width assumptions and the search checks at most O(sqrt(area)) widths. Auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Count assignments of plus and minus signs to nums whose signed sum equals target.
Idea: Recursively branch on adding or subtracting each number, memoizing states by index and current sum.
Technique and why it applies: Each number creates two possible next sums. At the end, the recursion returns one for a matching target and zero otherwise; cached results avoid recomputing the same state.
Invariant: dfs(i,sum_) is the number of ways to assign signs to nums[i:] that finish at target given the accumulated sum.
Edge cases: If abs(target) exceeds sum(nums), the code returns zero immediately. The snippet uses @cache without importing it, so it fails unless cache is defined externally.
Complexity: There are O(nS) possible index/sum states for total magnitude S, with two transitions each; memo space is O(nS), while the uncached search would be exponential.

Task and constraints: Count ways to assign plus or minus signs to nums so the result equals S.
Idea: Transform the sign-assignment problem into counting subsets whose sum is (total+S)/2, then use subset-sum dynamic programming.
Technique and why it applies: If P is the sum of positive-sign elements, then P-(total-P)=S, so P=(total+S)/2. The DP dictionary counts ways to form each sum using processed values.
Invariant: dp[x] stores the number of subsets from processed elements that sum to x.
Edge cases: The code returns zero if total<S or parity is wrong. For negative S, total<S is not an absolute-value check, but the derived target sum and dictionary lookup still govern whether a subset count is returned.
Complexity: The subset-sum loop costs O(nP) time and O(P) state space in the usual bounded-sum analysis, though defaultdict can hold only reached sums.

Task and constraints: Calculate the total duration during which poison is active after attacks at sorted timestamps.
Idea: Sum the non-overlapping contribution from each attack interval, capped by the gap to the next attack.
Technique and why it applies: The active interval from each timestamp contributes min(duration, nextTime-currentTime), and the final attack contributes the full duration. The earlier triple-quoted block is a string literal, so the active code is the concise loop after it.
Invariant: total accumulates poison time contributed by each attack without double-counting overlapping intervals.
Edge cases: Empty timeSeries returns duration because the final expression adds duration unconditionally; the standard problem guarantees at least one attack. This is the key assumption to note.
Complexity: The loop is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the input.

Task and constraints: Find the total time an enemy remains poisoned after a sequence of attacks.
Idea: Start with duration for every attack, then subtract overlap between adjacent poison intervals.
Technique and why it applies: Two attacks separated by less than duration overlap by duration-gap; if the gap is at least duration, no overlap is subtracted. The result therefore counts the union of all poison intervals.
Invariant: result begins as the sum of all individual durations and is reduced by each adjacent overlap.
Edge cases: An empty timeSeries returns zero because the initial product is zero. The method assumes attack timestamps are sorted in increasing order.
Complexity: One pass over adjacent timestamps gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: For each value in nums1, find the first greater value to its right in nums2, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Scan nums2 from right to left with a monotonic stack and record each value's next greater candidate.
Technique and why it applies: Values no greater than the current number are popped because they cannot be the next greater element for it or any earlier smaller candidate. The remaining stack top is the nearest greater value to the right.
Invariant: stack is decreasing from bottom to top in the traversal's candidate order, and dic maps processed values to their next greater value when one exists.
Edge cases: Values without a greater candidate are omitted from dic and default to -1. The usual problem guarantees distinct values in nums2, so value-keyed lookup is sufficient.
Complexity: Each nums2 value is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n+m) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return matrix elements in diagonal traversal order, alternating diagonal direction.
Idea: Enumerate diagonals by their index sum and reverse direction after each diagonal.
Technique and why it applies: total identifies cells with row+column equal to that diagonal index. flag determines whether the code reads mat[i][j] or mat[j][i], while the limits adapt to row and column counts.
Invariant: ans contains all cells from earlier diagonals in the required alternating order.
Edge cases: The code assumes mat is nonempty and has at least one column. The dimension-swapping logic is subtle for non-square matrices and should be tested on 1×N and N×1 matrices.
Complexity: Each matrix element is appended once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) output storage; the method also uses O(1) auxiliary variables.

Task and constraints: Traverse all elements of a rectangular matrix in alternating up-right and down-left diagonals.
Idea: Simulate movement with a direction vector and adjust coordinates when a matrix boundary is crossed.
Technique and why it applies: Each step appends the current cell, then advances along the diagonal. Boundary conditions clamp the row or column, move one extra step along the next diagonal, and flip direction.
Invariant: After each iteration, result contains the first i matrix entries in diagonal order and row/col is the next traversal position.
Edge cases: Empty matrices or empty first rows return an empty list. The boundary adjustment handles rectangular dimensions by checking row and column limits separately.
Complexity: Exactly mn iterations append one element each, so time is O(mn). The output uses O(mn) space, even though the author labels only O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Return words that can be typed using letters from only one row of the American keyboard.
Idea: Convert each word to lowercase characters and test whether its character set is contained in any one of the three row sets.
Technique and why it applies: Set intersection with a row set equals the whole word set precisely when every distinct letter belongs to that row. Original word casing is preserved in the result.
Invariant: Each word appended to res has all its letters contained in one keyboard row.
Edge cases: An empty word would pass the subset check for every row, but the standard constraints use nonempty words. The method handles uppercase letters through lower().
Complexity: For W words with total character count C, set construction and checks take O(C) expected time; row sets are constant-sized and per-word sets use O(length) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Filter words whose letters all come from one keyboard row.
Idea: For each word, test each keyboard row and append the word when all its lowercase letters occur in that row.
Technique and why it applies: all() checks every letter against the current row string. The method uses the original word for output, preserving capitalization.
Invariant: single_row_words contains only words that have passed at least one complete row membership check.
Edge cases: Empty words would satisfy all() vacuously and could be appended once for each of the three rows, creating duplicates; typical inputs contain nonempty words. The code does not break after the first matching row.
Complexity: Each word is tested against three rows, with membership in short strings, so time is O(C) for total input characters. Auxiliary space is O(1) beyond output.

Task and constraints: Return all words that can be typed using one keyboard row only.
Idea: Identify the row containing the first character, then ensure every character belongs to that row.
Technique and why it applies: The first character determines the only candidate row. If the later loop completes without break, the word is appended through the loop's else clause.
Invariant: A word is accepted only if every character passes membership in the selected row set.
Edge cases: Empty strings cause word[0] to raise IndexError, though the usual problem input uses nonempty words. Uppercase letters are normalized for membership while original strings are returned.
Complexity: Each character is checked once after a constant-size row lookup, giving O(C) time for total character count and O(1) auxiliary space apart from output.

Task and constraints: Maximize initial capital by completing at most k projects, each requiring capital and yielding a profit.
Idea: Sort projects by required capital, then repeatedly add all currently affordable projects to a max-heap and choose the most profitable.
Technique and why it applies: Negative profits turn Python's min-heap into a max-heap. Each chosen project's profit increases w, which may make additional projects affordable in the next iteration.
Invariant: The heap contains profits for projects affordable at the current capital that have not been chosen.
Edge cases: The shortcut when w>=max(capital) assumes every project is initially affordable and selects the k largest profits. max(capital) fails on empty input, though standard constraints are nonempty. Repeated pop(0) from projects shifts the list.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), but front removals can make project activation O(n²); heap operations add O(k log n). Space is O(n) for project pairs and heap.

Task and constraints: Choose up to k projects to maximize capital, with each project requiring no more than current capital.
Idea: Sort projects by required capital descending and use a max-heap for profits of all currently affordable projects.
Technique and why it applies: future[-1] is the least-capital remaining project because the list is reverse-sorted. Each iteration moves all affordable projects into curr, then chooses the highest profit by pushing negative values.
Invariant: curr contains all projects currently affordable but not selected, while future contains projects not yet affordable.
Edge cases: If no project is affordable, curr remains empty and capital is unchanged for that iteration. The code continues rather than stopping, but later iterations also cannot unlock projects without additional capital.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), and each project is pushed/popped at most once, giving O(n log n + k log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: For each element in a circular array, return the first strictly greater value encountered moving forward, or -1.
Idea: Scan the array twice backward and use a monotonic stack of candidate greater values.
Technique and why it applies: The doubled index range simulates circular wraparound. Values less than or equal to the current number are removed because they cannot be the next greater candidate; results are written only during the original-array pass.
Invariant: stack contains values that may be the next greater element for earlier positions in the circular scan.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty result because both loops are skipped. Equal values are popped because the desired value must be strictly greater.
Complexity: The doubled scan pushes and pops each value at most twice, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack/output space.

Task and constraints: Find each element's next greater value in the circular array, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Simulate two backward passes and maintain a monotonic decreasing stack of candidate values.
Technique and why it applies: Modulo indexing wraps the second pass to the start of nums. Candidates not greater than the current value are popped; the top then supplies the nearest greater value.
Invariant: The stack holds potential next-greater values from the suffix of the doubled traversal.
Edge cases: Empty nums yields an empty list without evaluating modulo inside the loop. Equal values are removed by <= so only strictly greater candidates remain.
Complexity: Each index is visited twice and each value is pushed and popped at most twice, so O(n) time and O(n) space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Convert athlete scores into medal names for the top three and numeric rank strings for all remaining athletes.
Idea: Sort (score,index) pairs by descending score and write each rank back to its original index.
Technique and why it applies: The sorted position determines rank, while the saved index restores the original input order. A try/except then replaces the first three rank strings with medal labels.
Invariant: ans at each original index contains the rank corresponding to that athlete's position in the sorted list.
Edge cases: The broad exception handler silently skips medal assignments if fewer than three athletes exist; the earlier numeric rank values remain correct. Equal scores are ordered by original index due to tuple sorting, although standard constraints specify distinct scores.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), and building and remapping ranks takes O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a positive integer equals the sum of its proper positive divisors.
Idea: Check divisors up to the square root and add each divisor together with its paired quotient.
Technique and why it applies: If i divides num, then i and num//i form a divisor pair. Summing both avoids scanning all integers up to num; the square root is added only once when it is an integer because the expression would otherwise double-count it only if i==num//i, which this code does not special-case.
Invariant: sum accumulates divisor pairs for factors i found from 2 through floor(sqrt(num)).
Edge cases: num=1 returns False explicitly. For a perfect square, the square-root divisor is added twice by sum += num//i + i, so the code incorrectly rejects some perfect-square perfect numbers if the root is a divisor; for standard perfect numbers this does not arise.
Complexity: The loop checks O(sqrt(num)) candidates and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
